After 8 days, the surviving mice were euthanized, and the weights of their organs, expressed as fractions of their body weights, were compared to those of 20 untreated male mice. 2. Mice treated with DBDC or TeBT exhibited enlarged livers, whereas those treated with TBTC did not. All three compounds caused an increase in spleen weight in the treated animals. 3. Brain weight in animals treated with TBTC or TeBT was greater than that of the control mice, but this effect was not observed in DBDC-treated mice. All compounds caused increases in kidney weight. 4. The results suggest that TeBT had effects similar to both DBDC and TBTC, but DBDC and TBTC differed in their toxic actions. 5. Kolia and Zalesov administered organotins via intraperitoneal injection to study the influence of chemical structure on the toxicities of the compounds. Eight hundred white mice weighing 16-17 g were used in a series of experiments where different groups were given one of 11 triarylor tetraaryltin derivatives in progressive doses until 100% fatality was achieved. 6. Animals were observed over a 10-day period or until 100% fatality occurred, and LD50 values were calculated using the Litchfield and Wilcoxon method. The LD50 values obtained are listed in Table XII-5, along with results of a statistical analysis comparing the toxicities of these compounds. 7. The results indicated that the toxicity of an organotin compound depended on both the type of anion and the organic side group. Halide salts appeared to be more toxic than the corresponding alkylated compounds, with bromides being more toxic than iodides. No chlorides were used. 8. Toxicity decreased with an increase in methylation of the aromatic radical. Tetraaryl derivatives were less toxic than their triaryl counterparts. Branching of the carbon chain in the alkyl group appeared to increase the toxicity of the compound. 9. Inhalation studies were conducted on rats under acute and chronic test conditions to evaluate the toxic properties of some triorganotins. Acute dust inhalation studies were performed for tri-n-butyltin fluoride (TnBTF) and triphenyltin fluoride (TPTF). 10. For TnBTF studies, young adult albino rats with an average weight of 165 g were divided into five groups of five males and five females. No control group was described in the studies. Animals were exposed to TnBTF in a test chamber for 4 hours, and mortality and behavioral reactions were noted. 11. Autopsy findings in some of these animals included mild to severe focal discoloration of the lungs and enlarged lungs. 12. The acute inhalation toxicity of dimethyltin dichloride (DMDC) vapor was evaluated in the presence of varying amounts of trimethyltin chloride (TMTC) contaminant, using young adult Charles River albino rats in groups of five males and five females. 13. Animals were exposed to DMDC for 1 hour, and mortality and behavioral reactions were observed for 21 days. Nominal vapor concentrations were based on weight loss of the test material and total volume of air used. 14. At the end of the 21-day period, animals were euthanized, and gross pathologic examination was conducted. At DMDC concentrations of 1,910 mg/cu m (1,031 mg/cu m as tin), 1,610 mg/cu m with 0.19% TMTC (870 mg/cu m as tin), and 2,640 mg/cu m with 0.87% TMTC (1,428 mg/cu m as tin), no deaths occurred. Body weight gains were normal, and autopsy revealed no gross pathologic alterations. 15. Hypoactivity and roughened fur were observed at these three concentrations; ptosis, enophthalmos, and salivation were also present at 2,640 mg/cu m with 0.87% TMTC. At a concentration of 2,110 mg/cu m with 2.09% TMTC (1,142 mg/cu m as tin), all animals died within 11 days, and hypoactivity, roughened fur, ptosis, enophthalmos, anesthesia, and tremors were observed in all animals. However, autopsy revealed no abnormalities attributable to DMDC toxicity. 16. With DMDC at a concentration of 4,080 mg/cu m with 3.59% TMTC (2,205 mg/cu m as tin), results were similar except that all animals died within 4 days. Similar test procedures were used to study the effects of short-term inhalation of DBDC and TMTC vapors. 17. Rats exposed to DBDC for 1 hour at a concentration of 1,470 mg/cu m (575.0 mg/cu m as tin) showed roughened fur, hypoactivity, ptosis, and salivation within the 14-day observation period. There were no deaths. Body weight gains were normal, and autopsy revealed no gross pathologic alterations. 18. All rats exposed to TMTC at a concentration of 8,890 mg/cu m (5,334 mg/cu m as tin) died on the first day; signs included hypoactivity, roughened fur, enophthalmos, ptosis, anesthesia, and dyspnea. Autopsy revealed no abnormalities attributable to TMTC. 19. Two vapor inhalation studies were conducted to determine the toxic effects of tributyltin chloride (TBTC) and tributyltin bromide (TBTB) on rats. Microscopic examinations were performed on the brain, lungs, liver, and kidneys. 20. Microscopic examination of the liver showed phagocytizing Kupffer cells, which were swollen and proliferating, small areas of necrosis, middle-grade fibrotic expansion of the periportal areas, and fine to medium droplets of fatty degeneration. 21. 22. The brain contained massive arterial hyperemia, pronounced cerebral edema, and cellular necrosis. These results indicated that severe brain damage caused by TBTC might be asymptomatic. 23. Iwamoto conducted a series of inhalation experiments to study the effects of TBTB on the reproductive functions of rats. The material used was a mixture of 81.2% TBTB with small amounts of dibutyltin dibromide and hydrocarbons. 24. The concentration of TBTB in the chamber was maintained by aeration of a TBTB mixture kept in the chamber. 25. 26. Three groups of five females exposed 2 hours/day for 2, 3, or 4 months, with mating occurring for the last 4 weeks, had pregnancy rates of 60%, 20%, and 0%. 27.
